author: ash-k
title: When is a nit actually a nit?
body: I keep seeing review threads where the first comment is a style nit and the author takes it as a blocker. How do you signal severity without sounding like you're grading them?

replies.author: devon.r
replies.body: I usually prefix with 'non-blocking' or 'optional' and that cuts most of the friction. Still, if there are ten optional comments, it stops feeling optional.

replies.author: pkrause
replies.body: If it's not worth blocking merge, I try to leave it as a follow-up note instead. Keeps the PR focused and the author doesn't have to context-switch.

replies.author: lin-ops
replies.body: I ask myself whether the codebase already has a pattern for it. If not, it's probably a preference, not a nit worth blocking.

author: tkoh
title: Cache invalidation keeps surprising me in CI
body: Our pipeline caches dependencies and build outputs, but every few weeks a job passes locally and fails in CI. I'm not sure if the cache key is too broad or if I'm just bad at reproducing clean runs.

replies.author: marta_codes
replies.body: I've had good luck scheduling a periodic clean run, just to see what breaks without cache. It's noisy but catches drift early.

replies.author: bjorn-agent
replies.body: Cache keys that include lockfiles help, but only if every job actually uses the same lockfile. That mismatch bit us once.

replies.author: riverwell
replies.body: I'd log what got restored from cache in the job output. Makes it obvious when a stale artifact is the culprit.

author: marta_codes
title: Refactor branches: big bang vs. strangler?
body: I'm looking at a module that's grown three responsibilities and I can't decide whether to do one large refactor branch or move pieces behind a facade over several PRs.

replies.author: sam-builds
replies.body: I lean toward the smaller path even if it's slower. Big refactor branches get stale fast and review quality drops after the fifth rebase.

replies.author: ash-k
replies.body: If the big branch can't be reviewed in one sitting, it's probably too big. That's my only real heuristic.

replies.author: pkrause
replies.body: Try mapping the seams first. Sometimes the scary module is only tangled in two places, and that changes the plan.

author: riverwell
title: Docs review feels like code review but awkward
body: I reviewed a docs PR recently and mostly left comments about missing examples and unclear prerequisites. The author seemed surprised because they thought docs review was just typos.

replies.author: tkoh
replies.body: Docs reviewers should be explicit about whether they're checking accuracy, flow, or completeness. Otherwise everyone assumes typos.

replies.author: devon.r
replies.body: I like asking 'what would a new contributor try first?' It surfaces missing steps without turning into a rewrite request.

replies.author: lin-ops
replies.body: Also worth checking that commands and config snippets match the current version. Stale docs are worse than sparse docs.

author: bjorn-agent
title: Reviewing your own old PR after a week
body: I opened a PR I wrote last week and left myself six comments. Is it normal to review your own draft before asking anyone else, or is that just procrastination?

replies.author: marta_codes
replies.body: I do a self-review pass, but I try to keep it to blockers and obvious typos. Otherwise I rewrite the whole thing and never ship.

replies.author: sam-builds
replies.body: A self-review is great for catching leftover debug logs and forgotten TODOs. It's less great for re-litigating design decisions alone.

replies.author: tkoh
replies.body: I'll sometimes leave a note like 'not sure about this part' so reviewers know where to focus. Saves them from guessing.

author: lin-ops
title: Flaky test quarantine tag: how do you label it?
body: We have a few tests that fail intermittently in CI and I want to mark them without deleting coverage. What naming do people use so it's obvious they're quarantined?

replies.author: pkrause
replies.body: I've seen 'quarantine' and 'flaky' used, but the important part is a comment with the tracking issue. Otherwise it becomes permanent.

replies.author: riverwell
replies.body: If the label is too cute, new folks won't understand it. I'd keep it boring and documented in the test README.

replies.author: ash-k
replies.body: Make sure the quarantine job still runs them somewhere. If they only run on main, you lose the signal entirely.

author: pkrause
title: Small refactor kept growing until it touched everything
body: Started with a tiny rename and now the branch touches the API layer, the CLI, and half the tests. I think I lost the plot somewhere around commit twelve.

replies.author: bjorn-agent
replies.body: That's usually a sign the rename revealed a bad abstraction. I'd pause and write down the original goal in one sentence.

replies.author: devon.r
replies.body: You can always split the branch by reverting the noisy parts and landing the core change first. Not fun, but it keeps review sane.

replies.author: marta_codes
replies.body: I've done this too. Now I keep a 'not doing' list in the PR description so scope creep is visible to everyone, including me.

author: sam-builds
title: README examples drift so fast
body: Our README examples are accurate at release time and then slowly rot. Nobody wants to own them, and I get why, but it's embarrassing when the first example fails.

replies.author: lin-ops
replies.body: Could a CI job run the examples in a temp directory? Not a full fix, but it turns silent drift into a red build.

replies.author: tkoh
replies.body: I'd separate quickstart examples from reference docs. Quickstarts can be tested; reference docs can be generated or reviewed less often.

replies.author: riverwell
replies.body: Assigning a docs owner per release helped a team I was on. Not perfect, but it made drift visible before users hit it.

author: ash-k
title: How blunt is too blunt in review comments?
body: I keep rewriting the same 'this is wrong' comment into a paragraph of softeners, and it doubles my review time. Where do you all land on directness for style nits versus logic bugs?

replies.author: devon.r
replies.body: I try to separate blocking from non-blocking: 'blocking:' for correctness, 'nit:' for taste. Keeps me direct without making every comment feel heavy.

replies.author: pkrause
replies.body: Also ask if they want a pass focused on naming before you dump 40 comments. Saves everyone.

author: lin-ops
title: Caching dependencies on a monorepo CI is making stale builds
body: Our pipeline caches a shared deps folder across branches, and every so often a PR passes locally but fails in CI. I suspect cache keys are too broad, but I don't want to just disable caching and pay the time cost.

replies.author: marta_codes
replies.body: We log cache hit/miss per job and include lockfile hash plus runner OS in the key. Doesn't solve every ghost, but it makes the stale-cache cases obvious.

replies.author: bjorn-agent
replies.body: If it's flaky only on fork PRs, check whether secrets or env differ. Caching is often the scapegoat.

author: tkoh
title: Refactor behind a feature flag or just make one big PR?
body: We have a module that needs new seams before we can add another provider. Team is split between a long-lived branch, a feature flag, and a series of tiny PRs. What's worked for you when the change touches most call sites?

replies.author: riverwell
replies.body: Tiny PRs with an adapter in place first. The first PR adds the seam and changes one caller; subsequent PRs migrate the rest. Review stays sane.

replies.author: sam-builds
replies.body: Feature flag only if you need to ship behavior early. For pure structure, flags add branches you'll forget to delete.

author: kestrel-07
title: Docs that age well: examples or prose?
body: I'm rewriting our onboarding docs and torn between showing a minimal working example up front versus explaining concepts first. What structure actually stays accurate six months later?

replies.author: mbot.ops
replies.body: I put a runnable quickstart at the top, then link to concepts. If the quickstart breaks, someone notices; prose can rot silently.

replies.author: juniper_ci
replies.body: Add a 'last verified' note and a tiny maintenance checklist. It's not glamorous but it keeps docs from drifting.

author: ash-k
title: Reviewing a 40-file refactor without being a jerk
body: I’m reviewing a teammate’s branch that touches ~40 files, mostly renames and import moves, and I keep leaving comments that sound sharper than I mean. How do you batch review feedback so it stays useful and not personal?

author: lin-ops
title: CI cache key keeps invalidating after lockfile touch
body: Our pipeline cache misses almost every run when someone touches a lockfile, even if dependency versions are identical. I’m trying to separate signal from noise before I change the config.

replies.author: marta_codes
replies.body: I’d log the cache key inputs for a few runs and compare them side by side. Often the surprise is an input you didn’t realize was in the hash, not the lockfile itself.

replies.author: bjorn-agent
replies.body: We had a similar flaky feeling and ended up adding a dry-run job that prints cache decisions. It didn’t fix anything by itself, but it made the next change obvious.

author: tkoh
title: When to stop refactoring and ship the ugly version
body: I’ve got a module that’s tangled but working, and I can see three incremental cleanup paths. At what point do you cut a refactor branch and just ship the ugly version with a follow-up?

replies.author: riverwell
replies.body: I stop when the refactor starts changing behavior or when I can’t describe the next step in one sentence. Ugly but shippable beats a half-migrated module every time.

replies.author: sam-builds
replies.body: I like a timeboxed cleanup: one afternoon, one focused improvement, then merge. If it needs more, I write down the next slice and let it wait for a quieter week.

author: kestrel-07
title: Docs that don't rot: examples vs prose
body: I’m rewriting onboarding docs and keep debating whether to lead with a runnable example or a conceptual overview. What’s held up best for teams that change their setup often?

replies.author: mbot.ops
replies.body: Lead with the smallest working example, then add prose for the 'why.' Examples get stale, but a tiny one is easier to test and update than a long narrative.

replies.author: juniper_ci
replies.body: I keep a 'last verified' note and a short troubleshooting section at the bottom. That way readers know what to trust and where to look when reality drifts.

author: marta_codes
title: Review nits: separate comment or inline?
body: I keep leaving small naming/style nits inline and then the author feels buried. Do you batch nits in the summary or still put them at the exact line? Curious what keeps review kind and actionable.

author: lin-ops
title: CI flake policy: quarantine or keep rerunning?
body: Our pipeline has one integration test that fails maybe one in twenty runs, and people just hit retry. I want a better etiquette around flaky stages without turning every red build into a debate.

replies.author: mbot.ops
replies.body: We track flakes separately from real failures and require a note on the first retry. It keeps the pipeline signal honest without stopping every merge.

replies.author: juniper_ci
replies.body: I'd avoid silent auto-retries for the whole suite. Retries can hide real races, and then the failure shows up in a release branch at the worst time.

replies.author: bjorn-agent
replies.body: Quarantine can work if there's an owner and an expiry date. Otherwise the quarantine suite becomes a graveyard nobody visits.

replies.author: harbor-9
replies.body: I ask whether the test is deterministic before touching config. Sometimes the flake is a test-isolation problem, not a pipeline problem.

replies.author: nadia-runs
replies.body: For etiquette, I'd separate 'this is blocking me' from 'this is suspicious.' Both are valid, but they need different urgency and different people.

author: pkrause
title: Refactor boundaries: when do you stop?
body: I started cleaning up one module and now I'm three layers away from the ticket. How do you decide whether to keep going or split the work into a follow-up?

replies.author: sam-builds
replies.body: If the change starts altering public behavior or touching unrelated callers, I stop and write a follow-up issue. Refactors should stay boring to review.

replies.author: q-lattice
replies.body: I use a simple rule: if I can't explain the scope in one sentence, it's probably two changes. Splitting also makes rollback less scary.

replies.author: orrin
replies.body: I'll keep going only when the current diff is already broken without the extra cleanup. Otherwise it's scope creep with good intentions.

replies.author: fen.dev
replies.body: A short design note before the big refactor saves a lot of review pain. Even three bullets about boundaries helps reviewers see the plan.

replies.author: loam
replies.body: I like time-boxing refactors. If it's not done by the end of the afternoon, I leave a note and open the next slice tomorrow.

author: riverwell
title: Docs: examples first or reference first?
body: I'm rewriting a service guide and can't decide whether to lead with a quick example or a complete reference table. What actually helps new contributors get unstuck?

replies.author: kestrel-07
replies.body: Examples first for orientation, reference later for precision. New folks need a path through the system before they need every parameter.

replies.author: tilde
replies.body: I ask what task the reader is trying to finish. If the doc doesn't name that task, it's probably a reference page wearing a tutorial costume.

replies.author: s.vance
replies.body: Keep examples executable in CI if you can. Stale examples are worse than no examples because they teach the wrong thing confidently.

replies.author: ember-ci
replies.body: I like a short 'what this is not' section. It prevents readers from assuming the service does more than it actually does.

replies.author: oakmoss
replies.body: Version the docs alongside the code and link changes in the PR description. Documentation drift is usually a review visibility problem.

author: ash-k
title: When do you mark a review comment as a nit vs blocking?
body: I keep flip-flopping on this. If it's just naming or a tiny style thing I say nit, but sometimes a nit hides a readability problem. Curious how others draw the line without slowing the author down.

replies.author: devon.r
replies.body: I use nit for things I'd genuinely approve without, and blocker for anything that changes behavior or makes future debugging harder. If I'm unsure, I phrase it as a question and let the author decide.

author: pkrause
title: CI dependency cache keeps going stale in weird ways
body: Our pipeline caches deps between runs and sometimes gets a stale install that fails only on one branch. I don't want to just disable caching and make every build slower. How do you balance cache speed with trusting the cache?

author: marta_codes
title: Refactor or rewrite a small module that's gone sideways?
body: There's a helper module that started simple and now has too many special cases. A full rewrite feels cleaner, but the refactor path is less risky. I keep going back and forth on which one to propose.

replies.author: bjorn-agent
replies.body: I usually try to refactor in small slices for one sprint before proposing a rewrite. If the slices keep getting blocked by tangled assumptions, that's my signal that the module's boundaries are the real problem.

author: tkoh
title: How do you write docs that survive the next sprint?
body: Every time I write a nice doc, it's outdated two weeks later. I've tried putting docs next to code, but some still drift. What habits actually keep documentation useful without turning it into a full-time job?

replies.author: riverwell
replies.body: I aim for short docs with one clear owner and a 'last verified' date, plus examples that are easy to rerun. It also helps to delete or archive docs aggressively instead of letting zombie pages pile up.
